To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cirrhotic ascites patients with refractory to diuresis also have blunted responses to marked elevations in plasma atrial natiuretic factor levels or to moderate intravenous volume expansion.

in cirrhotics with massive ascites, marked elevations in plasma ANF levels or massive intravascular volume expansions can improve the impaired ANF responsiveness of the kidney, which is responsible for refractory ascites.

(1) cirrhotic refractory ascites is associated with a blunted natriuresis to atrial natri­uretic factor (ANF) or to volume expansion, and (2) the natriuretic effect of ANF is enhanced by the combination of ANF and volume expansion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathogenesis of ascites in cirrhotics.
the pathogenesis and treatment of ascites in cirrhotics.
the pathophysiology and treatment of ascites and its complications in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the refractory ascites in patients with cirrhosis and ascites is due to an inability of the kidney to increase its capacity to excrete sodium and water.

the natriuretic effect of atrial natiuretic factor (ANF) infusion in cirrhotics with ascites is due to a direct effect of the hormone at the level of the kidney, and not to the volume expansion induced by its infusion.

the natriuresis of cirrhotic ascites patients with refractory to diuresis is not only due to the activation of the natriuretic hormone but also to the increased delivery of sodium filtrate to the cortical distally nephron.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the refractory ascites is a result of a combination of factors: 1. the cirrhosis itself, 2. the volume expansion, 3. the elevated plasma atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF).

the combination of head‐out water‐immersion and atrial natiuretic factor infusion is more effective than head‐out water­immersion and albumin infusion in the management of refractory ascites in alcoholic cirrhosis.
in patients with cirrhosis and massive ascites, the response to head‐out‐water‐immersion is blunted and the response to atrial natriuresis is blunted as well.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in patients with ascites, there are two ways to get the kidneys to excrete sodium.
the combination of volume expansion and atrial natiuretic factor is effective for the treatment of patients with ascites that is resistant to standard therapy.

the combination of head‐out water‐immersion and atrial natiuretic factor (ANF) infusion or head‐out water­immersion and albumin infusion can induce natriuresis in patients with cirrhosis and refractory ascites, and that this is achieved by way of an increase in distal tubular delivery of sodium, either with or without activation at the inner medulla of the distal tubular ANF receptor.
